Mere hardship, unequal financial consequences or the availability of a seemingly preferable arrangement does not, by itself, justify invalidating a taxing provision. Judicial restraint thus preserves Parliament’s legitimate fiscal discretion while ensuring that its exercise remains within constitutional limits.

Alternative Remedy in Fiscal Matters 27. Now, adverting to the respondents’ objection regarding the availability of an adequate alternative remedy, it is necessary to examine the nature of the grievance and the relief sought. The jurisdiction conferred by Article 199 is extraordinary and is not intended to provide an additional appellate forum whenever a taxpayer disputes the interpretation or application of a fiscal provision. Where the controversy can effectively be resolved through the machinery established by the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the statutory process must ordinarily be allowed to operate. Direct recourse to constitutional jurisdiction requires a sufficient justification for departing from that process; the taxpayer’s preference for adjudication by this Court cannot, by itself, supply such justification.

28. The statutory authorities examine the relevant returns, accounts, transactions and supporting documents, determine the applicable provisions and record findings upon which appellate scrutiny can proceed. This sequence enables the controversy to reach the appropriate judicial forum with an identified factual foundation and clearly formulated questions of law. Bypassing those stages may require the Constitutional Court to undertake the functions of an assessing or appellate authority upon a record that has not undergone the examination contemplated by the statute. The extraordinary jurisdiction must therefore be exercised with due regard to the respective functions assigned to the revenue authorities, appellate forums and this Court.

29. An alternative remedy is not rendered inadequate merely because its pursuit involves procedural steps, requires time, or may result in a decision adverse to the taxpayer. Its adequacy depends upon its capacity to address the grievance and provide effective relief. Equally, dissatisfaction with an order passed at one stage does not establish that the remaining statutory remedies are ineffective. Where a litigant has already invoked the statutory process, departure from that process must rest upon a compelling and justifiable reason rather than a desire to obtain a different forum. The principle reflected in the authorities reproduced above is that constitutional jurisdiction cannot ordinarily be invoked to interrupt or replace an available statutory course without demonstrating why that course is inadequate in the particular circumstances. In this regard, the Hon’ble Supreme Court, in Commissioner of Income Tax v. Hamdard Dawakhana (Waqf) (PLD 1992 SC 847), observed as follows: - “12. Before parting with the judgment we may observe that in cases where any party resorts to a statutory remedy against an order he cannot abandon or bypass it without any valid and reasonable cause and file Constitution petition challenging the same order. Such practice, in cases where statute provides alternate and efficacious remedy upto High Court, cannot be approved or encouraged. In a recent judgment of this Court in C.A. No. 79-K of 1991, one of us (Ajmal Mian, J.) in similar situation observed as follows:

"We may now revert to the question, whether the appellant was justified to file above Constitution petition against the order of the Tribunal instead of invoking section 136 of the Ordinance for making a reference to the High Court. According to Mr. Rehan Naqvi, a reference under the above provision would not have been adequate and efficacious remedy as it would have taken years before it could have been heard. The same could be true for a Constitution Petition. The tendency to bypass the remedy provided under the relevant statute and to press into service Constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court has developed lately, which is to be discouraged. However, in certain cases invoking of Constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court instead of availing of remedy provided for under the relevant statute may be justified, for example when the impugned order/action is palpably without jurisdiction and/or mala fide. To force an aggrieved person in such a case to approach the forum provided under the relevant statute may not be just and proper.

In the present case, the appellant had opted to avail of the hierarchy of forums provided for under the Ordinance upto the stage of filing of appeal before the Tribunal and, therefore, it would have been proper on the part of the appellant to have invoked section 136 of the Ordinance for making a reference to the High Court instead of filing a Constitutional petition. In our view, once a party opts to invoke the remedies provided for under the relevant statute, he cannot at his sweet will switch over to Constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court in the mid of the proceeding in the absence of any compelling and justifiable reason.”

30. Nevertheless, the respondents’ objection must be considered with an equally necessary qualification. A challenge to the constitutional validity of a statutory provision stands on a different footing from an allegation that the revenue authorities have misconstrued or misapplied it. A statutory tax forum cannot ordinarily grant the same relief as a constitutional Court where the relief sought is the invalidation of the governing legislation itself. Accordingly, the existence of an appellate hierarchy cannot, without examining the substance of the challenge, be treated as a complete answer to a properly raised question of legislative competence or infringement of a constitutional guarantee.

31. Conversely, the mere use of the expressions “unconstitutional”, “discriminatory” or “without lawful authority” does not transform an ordinary tax dispute into a substantive constitutional controversy. The Court must examine whether the petitioner identifies a defect in the legislation itself or principally contests the manner in which a valid provision has been applied to its transactions. In the present context, the distinction between the petitioner’s objection to the fiscal classification and any grievance concerning the computation, collection, adjustment or refund of tax is material. The constitutional objection requires examination against the relevant constitutional guarantee, whereas disputes concerning individual entitlement and the application of the statutory machinery must ordinarily be pursued before the forums competent to determine them. The same distinction applies to an allegation of absence of jurisdiction. An authority acting beyond the power conferred upon it presents a different question from an authority alleged to have reached an erroneous conclusion while exercising a power that it possesses. Every disputed assessment, demand or notice cannot be characterized as a jurisdictional nullity merely because the taxpayer denies liability. Otherwise, the exception would displace the ordinary rule and the statutory remedies would become dependent upon the terminology employed in the petition. The Court must therefore examine the asserted defect and the adequacy of the available remedy rather than accept the characterization of the impugned action at its face value. The distinction between a disputed exercise of statutory power and an action without jurisdiction is further illustrated by the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in M/s Payoneer Inc. v. Federation of Pakistan, wherein it observed: - “The High Court dealt with the issue of the impugned notice/show-cause notice very aptly. The registration alone under the ITO or the issuance of National Tax Number does not qualify as a coercive action against any entity, hence the contention of the petitioner that there should have been a prior notice before registration would not make any difference. The primary grievance of the petitioner, however, remained that the notice under section 114 of the ITO was issued, which may affect petitioner’s right, as the laws in respect of non-resident entity is well settled. The questions however remain if a better and statutory recourse is not available to avail the alternate writ jurisdiction. The simple answer is that such statutory recourse is available under ITO which has provided forums to resolve the raised questions. Mr. Awan has not been able to show if those forums are not efficacious.....

This Court in Geofizyka dealt with those issues once the tax reference was decided by the Islamabad High Court in Tax Reference No. 16 of 2005. Thus issuance of a show-cause notice cannot be equated to be one without jurisdiction hence the High Court was right in not exercising writ jurisdiction and left it to the petitioner to exhaust its remedy under the hierarchy of ITO.)”

32. Nor can a statutory provision restricting proceedings against orders passed under the Ordinance be understood as extinguishing jurisdiction conferred by the Constitution. Such a provision supports adherence to the prescribed statutory remedies, but the scope of constitutional jurisdiction remains governed by the Constitution itself. Likewise, the existence of factual controversy warrants restraint where its resolution requires examination of accounts, evidence or competing factual assertions; it does not automatically prevent consideration of a distinct constitutional question capable of determination upon admitted facts.

33. The governing approach is thus one of disciplined judicial restraint. Fiscal disputes must ordinarily proceed through the remedies established by law, while a substantive constitutional challenge must be examined within the limits of Article 199. The Court’s task is to preserve the statutory process without surrendering its constitutional responsibility, and to exercise extraordinary jurisdiction upon an established legal basis rather than as a substitute for the ordinary determination of tax liability. In case The State of Maharashtra and Ors. Vs. Greatship (India) Limited, reported as AIR 2022 SC 4408, the Indian Supreme Court held that: - “At the outset, it is required to be noted that against the assessment order passed by the Assessing Officer under the provisions of the MVAT Act and CST Act, the Assessee straightway preferred writ petition Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. It is not in dispute that the statutes provide for the right of appeal against the assessment order passed by the Assessing Officer and against the order passed by the first appellate authority, an appeal/revision before the Tribunal. In that view of the matter, the High Court ought not to have entertained the writ petition Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India challenging the assessment order in view of the availability of statutory remedy under the Act. At this stage, the decision of this Court in the case of Satyawati Tondon (supra) in which this Court had an occasion to consider the entertainability of a writ petition Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India by bypassing the statutory remedies, is required to be referred to. After considering the earlier decisions of this Court, in paragraphs 49 to 52, it was observed and held as under:

49. The views expressed in Titaghur Paper Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa MANU/SC/0317/1983 : (1983) 2 SCC 433 were echoed in CCE v. Dunlop India Ltd. MANU/SC/0169/1984 : (1985) 1 SCC 260 in the following words: (SCC p. 264, para 3)

3. Article 226 is not meant to short-circuit or circumvent statutory procedures. It is only where statutory remedies are entirely ill-suited to meet the demands of extraordinary situations, as for instance where the very vires of the statute is in question or where private or public wrongs are so inextricably mixed up and the prevention of public injury and the vindication of public justice require it that recourse may be had to Article 226 of the Constitution. But then the Court must have good and sufficient reason to bypass the alternative remedy provided by statute. Surely matters involving the revenue where statutory remedies are available are not such matters. We can also take judicial notice of the fact that the vast majority of the petitions Under Article 226 of the Constitution are filed solely for the purpose of obtaining interim orders and thereafter prolong the proceedings by one device or the other. The practice certainly needs to be strongly discouraged.”

34. The authorities discussed above establish the settled principle that, in fiscal matters, an adequate and efficacious statutory remedy must ordinarily be pursued before extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction is invoked. The machinery provided by the legislature for determining tax liability and redressing grievances cannot be bypassed merely because a taxpayer disputes the interpretation or application of the law or considers direct recourse to this Court more convenient. Departure from that course requires a compelling legal justification, such as an action palpably without jurisdiction, established mala fides, inadequacy of the statutory remedy, or a substantive challenge to the constitutional validity of the legislation. A constitutional objection must therefore be examined on its own merits, while grievances concerning assessment, computation, collection, adjustment or refund must ordinarily be addressed through the prescribed statutory process. This approach preserves both the effectiveness of the fiscal framework and the Court’s responsibility to enforce constitutional limitations.

35. For the foregoing reasons, the petitioner has failed to establish any constitutional infirmity in the impugned fiscal scheme. The distinction between manufacturing companies and Associations of Persons rests upon an intelligible differentia bearing a rational nexus with the objectives of incorporation, financial documentation and administration of tax liability. Similarity of manufacturing activity, individual compliance and comparative financial disadvantage do not, by themselves, render that classification violative of Article 25 of the Constitution. Nor has the petitioner established an unlawful deprivation of property under Articles 23 and 24 or an accrued entitlement to refund which would sustain its plea of unjust enrichment. The challenge to Section 153(3), particularly clause (a)(i) of its proviso, and the related provisions assailed in the petition therefore fails. Any distinct grievance concerning the computation, adjustment or refund of tax may be pursued through the statutory remedies available under the Ordinance, subject to the applicable legal requirements and the findings recorded herein. Consequently, the instant constitutional petition is DISMISSED. There shall be no order as to costs.

36. Before parting with this judgment, it is apposite to recall two observations which, read together, mark the boundaries within which this Court has approached the present petition. In McCulloch v. Maryland, 17 U.S. (4 Wheat.) 316, 431 (1819), Chief Justice Marshall acknowledged that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” More than a century later, Holmes J., dissenting in Panhandle Oil Co. v. Mississippi ex rel. Knox, 277 U.S. 218, 223 (1928), answered it in these words: “The power to tax is not the power to destroy while this Court sits.” The two statements describe complementary truths. The power to tax is a grave power, entrusted to the legislature and not to the courts. The courts do not exercise it, but they remain the guardians of the constitutional limits within which it must be exercised. Where a taxing provision is shown to be arbitrary, confiscatory or discriminatory in a manner the Constitution forbids, this Court will not hesitate to say so. Where, as here, the petitioner has demonstrated a financial disadvantage but not a constitutional infirmity, the choice between one method of taxation and other remains with Parliament. Holmes J. also recognized, in Compañía General de Tabacos de Filipinas v. Collector of Internal Revenue, 275 U.S. 87, 100 (1927) that “Taxes are what we pay for civilized society.” A taxpayer who has chosen a particular legal form for its business must accept the fiscal framework attached to that form, so long as the framework remains within constitutional bounds. The framework challenged here does.
